reasoning_summary: Step-by-step check. Lines 0002-0005: e={x,y} in T1; deleting an edge of a tree yields exactly two components A,B partitioning V with x in VA, y in VB, and e is the unique T1 edge crossing the (VA,VB) cut. Justified. Lines 0006-0011: T2 is a tree so there is a unique x-y path v0=x,...,vk=y; since x in VA and y in VB, there is a least j with v_{j-1} in VA and v_j in VB. Justified. Lines 0012-0013: f={v_{j-1},v_j} is a T2 edge crossing the cut. Justified. Lines 0014-0016 contain the only blemish: the assertion 'f cannot belong to T1' is not justified in the degenerate case e in T1 cap T2 (e.g. V={1,2}, T1=T2={{1,2}}, where the T2 path is the single edge e and hence f=e in T1). The stated reason only rules out a crossing T1 edge OTHER than e. However this claim is never used: neither tree-hood argument depends on it, and the edge counts (lines 0031-0032, 0049-0050) are decorative since both parts independently establish connected + acyclic. Lines 0034-0046: T1\{e} is the disjoint union of trees A and B; f joins VA to VB, so the result is connected, and since no A-B path exists in T1\{e}, adding f creates no cycle. Correct (and trivially correct if f=e, giving back T1). Lines 0048-0060: f lies on the unique T2 path from x to y, so T2\{f} separates x from y; T2\{f} is acyclic as a subgraph of a tree, and adding e={x,y} joins its two components, giving connected and acyclic. Correct, and the uniqueness-of-paths justification for 'no x-y path remains' is valid. Lines 0061-0065 conclude correctly. The theorem is fully established; the only defect is a superfluous, unused overstatement at line 0014, so I do not stop there.
